source_group: The maritime calendar and the peninsular forest
summary_findings: TWO RESULTS, AND THE SECOND IS A NEGATIVE THAT EXPLAINS SEVERAL OTHERS. FIRST: THE MALDIVE AND MINICOY SKY IS THE SAME TWENTY-SEVEN ASTERISMS, RE-INDEXED AGAINST THE MONSOON. Maniku's Dhivehi vocabulary gives every one of the twenty-seven a headword with its stars in Bayer designations — and defines each not by its place in the moon's circuit but by its number within a monsoon: eighteen nakaiy of the hulhangu or south-west monsoon, from Assidha (Aśvinī) to Dhosha (Jyeṣṭhā), then nine of the iruvai or north-east, from Mula (Mūla) to Reyva (Revatī), 'the ninth and the last'. Every other language in this database that has the twenty-seven has them as the moon's stations counted once round; Divehi keeps the names and re-hangs them on the SUN and the wind. That is a sailor's calendar — it answers when the season turns, not where the moon is — and it is why Mūla, an unremarkable nineteenth in the Sanskrit list, is here the hinge of the year. The system was administered: ނަކަތްޗާ nakaiychaa, 'the nakaiy man', was an office at the Sultan's palace. And it was kept true to the sun by a twenty-eighth, އަވިހި AVIHI, a variable intercalary nakaiy now disused — the only place in this database where a vernacular calendar's leap mechanism is recorded. Minicoy (Maliku), Indian territory in Lakshadweep, speaks this language and uses this calendar. SECOND: THE CHOLANAIKKANS HAVE NO CONSTELLATIONS, AND THE RECORDERS SAY WHY IN THEIR FIRST SENTENCE — 'absence of farming activities made sky-watching a never compelling affair'. They are forest foragers of fewer than two hundred people in the Nilambur reserves. They have two words for 'star', Koram and Udumbam, and identify no star and no pattern whatever: shown the night sky in the Kozhikode planetarium, the party smiled and walked out. They do not know that the sun rises at different points through the year and so do not connect it with the seasons. THIS IS THE CONTROL CASE FOR THE WHOLE DATABASE. tribal.json already had Radcliffe-Brown's flat statement that constellations are not recognised in the North Andaman, recorded as a result rather than a gap; here the same result comes with a cause attached, and it is the cause the rest of this compilation would predict. Every figure in this database that carries a story belongs to a community that plants something — the cot and the three thieves, the plough with its two bullocks and its ploughman, the sowing-star, the threshing floor, the seed drill, the Pleiades that say when to sow. What the Cholanaikkans do have is a meteor, Katui, 'embers of the fire sent by the gods' — and a meteor needs no calendar. THE FISHERMEN'S MEASURES WERE NOT FOUND, AND THAT IS THE WAVE'S REAL FAILURE. The plan aimed at the fist-and-finger star-altitude systems reported for the Indian Ocean — kai kanakku in Lakshadweep and Malabar, viral kanakku in Tamil Nadu, dhru in Gujarat — and the lexicographic route does not reach them. The Tamil Lexicon has கைக்கணக்கு kai-k-kaṇakku only as a memorandum of accounts and has no விரற்கணக்கு at all; its navigational vocabulary is generic (மாலுமி mālumi 'pilot, navigator', from the Arabic muʿallim that also names the Kutchi mālam manuals; சுக்கானி cukkāni 'helmsman'; காந்தப்பெட்டி kānta-p-peṭṭi 'magnet box', the mariner's compass). The one real find is சங்கு caṅku, the gnomon that measures the sun's altitude by its shadow — the classical instrument, not a rule of thumb, and the second entry in this database's 'Measuring the sky' object after Mizo suk-chen. A proper pass at the fist-measures needs the maritime literature (Tibbetts on Arab navigation, the Kutchi mālam manuscripts), all of it in copyright and none of it reached here. PENINSULAR TRIBAL, LARGELY DRY AGAIN. Thurston's volume II was downloaded and searched for nine sky terms and returned one hit, on 'constellation', with no star name — confirming from a second volume what tamil.json found in the other six. No Sora, Savara, Kui, Irula, Kurumba, Chenchu or Koya source could be obtained: the dictionary and monograph identifiers tried on archive.org returned empty metadata, and none of those languages is on DSAL. The Vahia and Halkare Pardhi paper, listed in the plan since Wave 1, is still not obtained.

entries.usage_note: Maniku gives every one of the twenty-seven asterisms its own headword, and each is defined not by its place in the moon's circuit but by its number within a monsoon: eighteen nakaiy of the hulhangu or south-west monsoon, running from Assidha (Aśvinī) to Dhosha (Jyeṣṭhā), then nine of the iruvai or north-east monsoon, from Mula (Mūla) to Reyva (Revatī), 'the ninth and the last'. Each entry names the stars in Bayer designations.
entries.citation: Hassan Ahmed Maniku, A Concise Etymological Vocabulary of Dhivehi Language, Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society of Sri Lanka, Special Volume XLIV (Colombo, 2000), s.v. nakaiy, p. 187
entries.notes: In copyright, so the finding is paraphrased and `quote` is null. THE FINDING OF THIS WAVE, AND IT IS STRUCTURAL RATHER THAN LEXICAL. Every other language in this database that has the twenty-seven asterisms has them as the moon's stations, counted once round in order. Divehi keeps the same twenty-seven names but re-indexes them against the SUN and the two monsoons — so the year has two halves and the asterisms are numbered within each. That is a sailor's and a fisherman's calendar: it answers when the wind turns, not where the moon is. The individual names are Sanskritic through Sinhala and a table of them would be the 'large and nearly uninformative' thing FORMAT.md warns against, so only the system and the five structurally interesting members are entered here. Minicoy in Lakshadweep, Indian territory, speaks this language and uses this calendar.

entries.notes: In copyright, so the finding is paraphrased and `quote` is null. A LEAP-ASTERISM. Twenty-seven asterisms will not tile a solar year, and the Divehi solution was a twenty-eighth of variable length inserted to keep the two in step — the same job Abhijit does as the intercalated asterism in the Sanskrit scheme, but here stated as a calendrical mechanism rather than a name. Nothing else in this database records how a vernacular calendar was kept true to the sun.

The Munda, Dravidian and Tibeto-Burman languages in this database make a meteor star-excrement; Mizo makes it shoot, Nepali makes it burst, Chowra makes it rubbish thrown out. Divehi makes it a stone struck from a fire — the only language here that names the material rather than the motion. Compare the Cholanaikkan Katui in this file, 'embers of the fire sent by the gods'.

entries.usage_note: The two words the Cholanaikkans gave for 'star'. The recorders add that they identify no individual stars and know no star patterns at all: shown the night sky in the Kozhikode planetarium, the party smiled and walked out.
entries.citation: M. N. Vahia, V. S. Ramachandran, Jayant Gangopadhyay and Justin Joseph, 'Astronomy of Cholanaikkan tribe of Kerala', arXiv:1702.04149 (2017), §9 'Their astronomy', p. 7
entries.notes: In copyright, so the finding is paraphrased and `quote` is null. THE SECOND COMMUNITY IN THIS DATABASE WITH NO CONSTELLATIONS, AND THE ONE THAT EXPLAINS THE FIRST. tribal.json records Radcliffe-Brown's flat statement that individual stars and constellations are not recognised in the North Andaman. Here the same result comes with a reason attached, and the recorders state it in their first sentence: the absence of farming made sky-watching a never compelling affair. The Cholanaikkans are forest foragers of fewer than two hundred people. Every constellation in this database that has a story attached to it belongs to a community that plants something — the cot and the thieves, the plough and the bullocks, the sowing-star and the harvest implement. This is the control case.

entries.usage_note: Nyaram is close to Malayalam ñāyar, which is Sunday. They are glad when the sun is overhead, feeling protected by it, and bury their dead with the head to the west, the end of life as against its beginning.
entries.citation: M. N. Vahia, V. S. Ramachandran, Jayant Gangopadhyay and Justin Joseph, 'Astronomy of Cholanaikkan tribe of Kerala', arXiv:1702.04149 (2017), §9 'Their astronomy', p. 7
entries.notes: In copyright, so the finding is paraphrased and `quote` is null. The one celestial body that carries any weight for them, and it carries it as a protector and as a direction for the dead rather than as a calendar. The recorders note they do not know that the sun rises at different points on the horizon through the year, and so do not connect it with the seasons — which is the same absence again.

entries.citation: M. N. Vahia, V. S. Ramachandran, Jayant Gangopadhyay and Justin Joseph, 'Astronomy of Cholanaikkan tribe of Kerala', arXiv:1702.04149 (2017), §9 'Their astronomy', p. 7

The etymology is the recorders' own, from Malayalam rather than from Cholanaikkan, and the phrase may be a Malayalam description reported back rather than a Cholanaikkan name — hence 'likely'. Recorded because the image is exact: a running coconut-leaf torch is what a fireball looks like.

entries.sky_object: a gnomon for measuring the altitude of the sun by the length of its shadow
entries.usage_note: The Tamil Lexicon's second sense at this headword, after 'stake, peg, spike'.
entries.citation: Tamil Lexicon, published under the authority of the University of Madras (Madras, 1924-1939), s.v. சங்கு⁵, vol. III p. 1229
entries.quote: சங்கு⁵ caṅku , n . šaṅku . 1. Stake, peg, spike; முளை. 2. Gnomon or perpendicular column for measuring the altitude of the sun by the length of its shadow; நிழலினாற் பொழுதறிதற்காக நேரா…
entries.notes: The second entry in the database's 'Measuring the sky' object, which Mizo suk-chen opened in northeast.json. The two are opposite methods: the Mizo hold up a pestle against the sky and count its lengths, the Tamil plant a post and read its shadow. The word is Sanskrit śaṅku and the instrument is the classical one, so this is the learned tradition rather than a fisherman's rule of thumb — see the summary on what could not be found of the latter.

caveats: Maniku (2000) and the Cholanaikkan paper (2017) are both in copyright: their findings are paraphrased and `quote` is null. The one quoted entry in this file is the Tamil gnomon from the Madras Tamil Lexicon, quoted verbatim from DSAL's page view as the rest of tamil.json is.

ONLY SEVEN OF THE TWENTY-SEVEN NAKAIY ARE ENTERED, AND THAT IS AN EDITORIAL DECISION, NOT AN OMISSION. Maniku gives all twenty-seven and this file could have listed them; FORMAT.md's opening argument is that a table of the inherited asterism names in one more language would be 'large, easy to compile, and nearly uninformative'. What is informative here is the SYSTEM — the re-indexing against the monsoons, the intercalary avihi, the court office — and the members whose position in it is structurally interesting: the first and last of the north-east monsoon, and three whose star-lists or glosses add something. The other twenty are named in the nakaiy entry's usage note and can be read in Maniku at the pages cited from it.

Divehi is included on the same footing as Sinhala, which this database has carried from the start: the language of Minicoy (Maliku) in Lakshadweep is Mahl, which is Divehi, and the nakaiy calendar is used there. The `region` field says so on every entry. A reader who wants the database confined to the Republic of India should filter on region, not on language.

One error of Maniku's is reproduced rather than corrected: at މިއަހެލިއަ miahelia he lists 'Lambda, Phi one, Aldebaran and Phi two in Orionis', putting Aldebaran in Orion where it is α Tauri. The group he means is not in doubt and the slip is his; the entry says so.

The Cholanaikkan entries carry NO iso639_3 code. Cholanaikkan is a Dravidian speech of the Nilambur forests with fewer than two hundred speakers and no code the compiler could assign with confidence; a wrong code is worse than none, so the field is null and the region field carries the identification. This is the only language in the database without a code.

`ChootuPaayuka` is graded `likely` because the recorders derive it from Malayalam — cūṭṭu, a torch of dried coconut leaves, and pāyuka, 'to run fast' — and it may therefore be a Malayalam description offered to them rather than a Cholanaikkan name. The distinction matters in a community this small and this closely surrounded by Malayalam, and it is recorded rather than resolved.

The Cholanaikkan negative is entered as a usage note on the word for 'star' rather than as a free-standing claim, because that is where a reader will meet it. The full statement — no identified stars, no patterns, the planetarium visit, the sun not connected with the seasons — is in the summary findings, which is where this database keeps its negatives.

The fist-and-finger measures are recorded as NOT FOUND rather than as absent. The Tamil Lexicon was searched for கைக்கணக்கு and விரற்கணக்கு and for navigation, mariner, sailor, helmsman, compass, fathom and altitude; the first exists only as a book-keeping term and the second not at all. That is a fact about the lexicon, which is a literary and not a maritime record. The practice is well attested in the secondary literature and this database has simply not reached a citable primary source for it.
